notes.front: What are earnings and profits (E&P), and why do they matter for distributions?
notes.back: A corporation’s earnings measure; a distribution from current or accumulated E&P is reported to the shareholder as a dividend.
notes.explanation: Publication 542 treats a corporate distribution as generally coming out of earnings and profits first.
notes.example: Like a reservoir of profits: what a corporation pays out is a dividend as long as the reservoir has water in it.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Reporting Dividends and Other Distributions”, p. 17
notes.evidence: A corporate distribution to a shareholder is generally treated as a distribution of earnings and profits. Any part of a distribution from either current or accumulated earnings and profits is reported to the shareholder as a dividend.

notes.front: What is the dividends-received deduction (DRD)?
notes.back: A deduction a corporation takes for part (or all) of the dividends it receives from other corporations, at 50%, 65% or 100%.
notes.explanation: The Form 1120 instructions give each rate its own line on Schedule C, depending on ownership.
notes.example: Like a company that holds shares in a supplier deducting part of the dividends it receives before its tax is figured.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule C. Dividends, Inclusions, and Special Deductions”, p. 19
notes.evidence: Dividends received on certain debt-financed stock acquired after July 18, 1984, are not entitled to the full 50% or 65% dividends-received deduction under section 243 or 245(a).

notes.front: What is a stock redemption, and how is it generally treated?
notes.back: A corporation buying back a shareholder’s stock; it is treated as a sale or trade unless it is a dividend or other distribution.
notes.explanation: Whether it is a sale or a dividend depends on the circumstances in each case.
notes.example: Like a family company buying back all the shares of a founder who is retiring.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Redemption of stock”, p. 54
notes.evidence: A redemption of stock is treated as a sale or trade and is subject to the capital gain or loss provisions unless the redemption is a dividend or other distribution on stock.

notes.front: What is a complete liquidation, from a shareholder’s point of view?
notes.back: The winding up of a corporation, during which shareholders receive liquidating distributions: at least in part a return of capital.
notes.explanation: Liquidating distributions may come in one or more instalments and are reported on Form 1099-DIV.
notes.example: Like a closing company selling everything and sharing out the cash among its shareholders.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Liquidating Distributions”, p. 31
notes.evidence: Liquidating distributions, sometimes called liquidating dividends, are distributions you receive during a partial or complete liquidation of a corporation. These distributions are, at least in part, one form of a return of capital.

notes.front: What is the accumulated earnings tax?
notes.back: A 20% tax that may apply when a corporation lets earnings accumulate beyond the reasonable needs of the business.
notes.explanation: Accumulating for expansion or other bona fide business reasons is allowed.
notes.example: Like a charge on a company that keeps piling up cash it does not need, instead of paying dividends its owners would be taxed on.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Accumulated Earnings Tax”, p. 15
notes.evidence: if a corporation allows earnings to accumulate beyond the reasonable needs of the business, it may be subject to an accumulated earnings tax of 20%.

notes.front: What is the corporate alternative minimum tax (CAMT)?
notes.back: A tax for tax years beginning after 2022, based on the adjusted financial statement income of an applicable corporation.
notes.explanation: Unless an exclusion applies, a corporation uses Form 4626 to see whether it is an applicable corporation and to figure the tax.
notes.example: Like a floor built from the profits a very large company reports to investors, rather than its taxable income.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax (CAMT)”, p. 15
notes.evidence: For tax years beginning after 2022, section 55 of the Internal Revenue Code imposes a new corporate alternative minimum tax (CAMT) based on the adjusted financial statement income of an applicable corporation.

notes.front: What is a section 351 exchange?
notes.back: A transfer of property to a corporation for its stock, after which the transferors control it; the exchange is usually not taxable.
notes.explanation: It applies to one transferor or a group, and to new or existing corporations.
notes.example: Like a sole proprietor moving the business’s van and tools into a new corporation in return for all its shares.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Property Exchanged for Stock”, p. 3
notes.evidence: If you transfer property (or money and property) to a corporation in exchange for stock in that corporation (other than nonqualified preferred stock), and immediately afterward you are in control of the corporation, the exchange is usually not taxable.

notes.front: In a section 351 exchange, what is boot?
notes.back: Money or property other than stock received in the exchange; it can make you recognise gain.
notes.explanation: Gain is recognised only up to the money plus the fair market value of the other property.
notes.example: Like getting shares plus a cheque when you hand property to your corporation: the cheque is the boot.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Money or other property received”, p. 28
notes.evidence: If, in an otherwise nontaxable exchange of property for corporate stock, you also receive money or property other than stock, you may have to recognize gain.

notes.front: What is a controlled group, and what must its component members file?
notes.back: A group of corporations linked by common ownership (parent–subsidiary, brother–sister or combined); members file Schedule O to apportion certain tax benefits.
notes.explanation: The members are limited in how they use certain tax benefits.
notes.example: Like a family of companies owned by the same people, which must share certain tax benefits instead of each claiming them in full.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule O (Form 1120) (Rev. December 2018), “Purpose of Schedule”, p. 1
notes.evidence: A corporation that is a component member (defined below) of a controlled group must use Schedule O to report the apportionment of certain tax benefits between all component members of the group.

notes.front: What is a closely held corporation?
notes.back: Not a personal service corporation; five or fewer individuals own over 50% of its stock value at any time in the year’s last half.
notes.explanation: Ownership can be direct or indirect, and “individual” includes certain trusts and private foundations.
notes.example: Like a manufacturing company where three siblings own 70% of the shares.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Closely held corporations”, p. 3
notes.evidence: At any time during the last half of the tax year, more than 50% of the value of its outstanding stock is, directly or indirectly, owned by or for five or fewer individuals.

notes.front: What is a personal service corporation (PSC)?
notes.back: A corporation whose principal activity in the testing period is personal services, performed substantially by employee-owners who own over 10% of its stock.
notes.explanation: All three requirements must be met; the testing period is generally the prior tax year.
notes.example: Like an engineering firm whose engineers own the company and do most of its work.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Personal service corporations”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Its principal activity during the "testing period" is performing personal services (defined later). Generally, the testing period for any tax year is the prior tax year.

notes.front: When is Form 1120 generally due?
notes.back: By the 15th day of the 4th month after the tax year ends.
notes.explanation: A corporation whose fiscal year ends 30 June files by the 15th day of the 3rd month instead.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “When To File”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Generally, a corporation must file its income tax return by the 15th day of the 4th month after the end of its tax year.

notes.front: A corporation’s tax year ends 31 October 2025. By what date is its Form 1120 due, before extensions or weekend rules?
notes.back: A: 15 February 2026.
notes.choices:
A) 15 February 2026
B) 15 January 2026
C) 15 April 2026
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: that is the 3rd month, used only for a 30 June year end. C is wrong: that is the date for a calendar-year corporation.
notes.explanation: Count four months after October: November, December, January, February; then the 15th.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “When To File”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Generally, a corporation must file its income tax return by the 15th day of the 4th month after the end of its tax year.

notes.front: A corporation’s tax year ends 30 June 2025. When is its Form 1120 due, before extensions or weekend rules?
notes.back: 15 September 2025: the 15th day of the 3rd month.
notes.explanation: The 30 June year end is the exception to the usual 4th-month rule.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “When To File”, p. 4
notes.evidence: However, a corporation with a fiscal tax year ending June 30 must file by the 15th day of the 3rd month after the end of its tax year.

notes.front: What is the penalty for filing Form 1120 late without reasonable cause?
notes.back: 5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part month late, up to 25%.
notes.explanation: A minimum penalty applies to returns more than 60 days late.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Late filing of return”, p. 6
notes.evidence: A corporation that does not file its tax return by the due date, including extensions, may be penalized 5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month the return is late, up to a maximum of 25% of the unpaid tax.

notes.front: A corporation files its 2025 Form 1120 (due in 2026) 70 days late, owing $300 of tax, with no reasonable cause. What late-filing penalty applies?
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the minimum is the smaller of the tax due or $525. C is wrong: that is 5% × 3 months, below the minimum.
notes.explanation: 5% × 3 months (a part month counts) × $300 = $45. But a return due in 2026 and over 60 days late has a minimum of the smaller of the tax due or $525: $300.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Late filing of return”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The minimum penalty for a tax return required to be filed in 2026 that is more than 60 days late is the smaller of the tax due or $525.

notes.front: At what rate do corporations, including qualified personal service corporations, figure their income tax?
notes.back: 21% of taxable income.
notes.explanation: A member of a controlled group also completes Schedule O to apportion certain tax benefits.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Tax Rates”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Corporations, including qualified personal service corporations, figure their tax by multiplying taxable income by 21% (0.21).

notes.front: A C corporation has 2025 taxable income of $400,000 and no credits. What is its regular income tax?
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: that is 20%. B is wrong: that is 35%, not the flat corporate rate.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule J, Line 1a”, p. 22
notes.evidence: income (page 1, line 30) by 21% (0.21). Enter this amount on line 1a.

notes.front: When must a corporation generally make estimated tax instalment payments?
notes.back: If it expects its estimated tax for the year to be $500 or more.
notes.explanation: Missing instalments can bring an underpayment penalty.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Estimated Tax”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Generally, a corporation must make installment payments if it expects its estimated tax for the year to be $500 or more.

notes.front: A corporation’s tax year runs 1 October to 30 September. When are its estimated tax instalments due?
notes.back: B: 15 January, 15 March, 15 June and 15 September.
notes.choices:
A) 15 April, 15 June, 15 September and 15 December
B) 15 January, 15 March, 15 June and 15 September
C) 15 October, 15 January, 15 April and 15 July
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: those are the dates for a calendar-year corporation. C is wrong: instalments fall in the 4th, 6th, 9th and 12th months.
notes.explanation: Counting from October as month 1: January is the 4th, March the 6th, June the 9th and September the 12th.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “When to pay estimated tax”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Installment payments are due by the 15th day of the 4th, 6th, 9th, and 12th months of the corporation's tax year.

notes.front: For tax year 2025, what penalty relief applies to estimated tax attributable to a CAMT liability?
notes.back: The section 6655 underpayment penalty is waived for estimated tax attributable to CAMT.
notes.explanation: The Form 1120 instructions continue this waiver for tax year 2025, citing Notice 2025-27.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “What’s New”, p. 1
notes.evidence: For tax year 2025, the IRS will continue to waive the penalty imposed under section 6655 for failure to make estimated tax payments attributable to a CAMT liability.

notes.front: What happens to the part of a distribution that is not from earnings and profits?
notes.back: It reduces the shareholder’s adjusted basis in the stock; any excess over basis is gain, usually capital gain.
notes.explanation: Only the part from current or accumulated earnings and profits is a dividend.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Reporting Dividends and Other Distributions”, p. 17
notes.evidence: Any part of a distribution that is not from earnings and profits is applied against and reduces the adjusted basis of the stock in the hands of the shareholder. To the extent the balance is more than the adjusted basis of the stock, the shareholder has a gain (usually a capital gain)

notes.front: A corporation with $30,000 of E&P distributes $50,000 to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $15,000. How is the $50,000 treated?
notes.back: B: $30,000 dividend, $15,000 return of basis, $5,000 gain.
notes.choices:
A) $50,000 dividend
B) $30,000 dividend, $15,000 return of basis, $5,000 gain
C) $30,000 dividend, $20,000 gain
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: only the part from E&P is a dividend. C is wrong: the non-dividend part first reduces stock basis.
notes.explanation: Dividend up to E&P ($30,000); the remaining $20,000 cuts basis from $15,000 to zero; the last $5,000 is gain, usually capital.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Reporting Dividends and Other Distributions”, p. 17
notes.evidence: Any part of a distribution that is not from earnings and profits is applied against and reduces the adjusted basis of the stock in the hands of the shareholder.

notes.front: If current-year E&P (before distributions) exceeds all the year’s distributions, how are they treated?
notes.back: All of them are distributions of current-year earnings and profits.
notes.explanation: Current-year E&P is figured at the close of the year without reducing it for the year’s distributions.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Current year earnings and profits”, p. 18
notes.evidence: If a corporation's earnings and profits for the year (figured as of the close of the year without reduction for any distributions made during the year) are more than the total amount of distributions made during the year, all distributions made during the year are treated as distributions of current year earnings and profits.

notes.front: What are accumulated earnings and profits?
notes.back: Earnings and profits the corporation accumulated before the current year.
notes.explanation: They come into play when the year’s distributions exceed current-year E&P.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Accumulated earnings and profits”, p. 18
notes.evidence: Accumulated earnings and profits are earnings and profits the corporation accumulated before the current year.

notes.front: Current-year E&P is $12,000; accumulated E&P is $50,000. The corporation makes two $10,000 distributions. How much of each comes from current-year E&P?
notes.back: A: $6,000 each; the other $4,000 of each is from accumulated E&P.
notes.choices:
A) $6,000 each; the other $4,000 of each is from accumulated E&P
B) $10,000 of the first, $2,000 of the second
C) All $20,000, since total E&P is $62,000
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: current-year E&P is spread proportionately, not first come, first served. C is wrong: current-year E&P alone is only $12,000.
notes.explanation: $12,000 ÷ $20,000 = 0.6; 0.6 × $10,000 = $6,000 from current E&P per distribution; $4,000 each from accumulated.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Accumulated earnings and profits”, p. 18
notes.evidence: If a corporation's current year earnings and profits (figured as of the close of the year without reduction for any distributions made during the year) are less than the total distributions made during the year, part or all of each distribution is treated as a distribution of accumulated earnings and profits.

notes.front: A shareholder-employee who works 10 hours a week is paid a $400,000 salary; similar work would earn about $60,000. What may the excess be treated as?
notes.back: A distribution to the shareholder-employee.
notes.explanation: The excessive part of an unreasonably high salary, given the services actually performed, may be recharacterised.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Unreasonable salaries”, p. 17
notes.evidence: If a corporation pays an employee who is also a shareholder a salary that is unreasonably high considering the services actually performed by the shareholder-employee, the excessive part of the salary may be treated as a distribution to the shareholder-employee.

notes.front: A corporation lends its shareholder money interest-free. What may be treated as a distribution?
notes.back: The interest not charged.
notes.explanation: The same applies where interest is charged below the applicable federal rate.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Constructive Distributions: Below-market loans”, p. 17
notes.evidence: If a corporation gives a shareholder a loan on which no interest is charged or on which interest is charged at a rate below the applicable federal rate, the interest not charged may be treated as a distribution to the shareholder.

notes.front: A corporation writes off a $25,000 loan it made to a shareholder, who repays nothing. How is the $25,000 treated?
notes.back: As a distribution to the shareholder.
notes.explanation: Cancelling a shareholder’s debt without repayment is one of the constructive distributions Publication 542 lists.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Constructive Distributions: Corporation cancels shareholder's debt”, p. 17
notes.evidence: If a corporation cancels a shareholder's debt without repayment by the shareholder, the amount canceled is treated as a distribution to the shareholder.

notes.front: A corporation sells its individual shareholder a car worth $50,000 for $30,000. What is treated as a distribution?
notes.choices:
A) $50,000
B) $20,000
C) Nothing, because it was a sale
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the shareholder paid $30,000 of the value. C is wrong: a bargain sale to a shareholder can be a distribution.
notes.explanation: The excess of fair market value over the price paid: $50,000 − $30,000 = $20,000.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Transfers of property to shareholders for less than FMV”, p. 17
notes.evidence: For a shareholder who is not a corporation, if the FMV of the property on the date of the sale or exchange exceeds the price paid by the shareholder, the excess is treated as a distribution to the shareholder.

notes.front: What is the amount of a distribution of property, and what is the shareholder’s basis in the property?
notes.back: Money plus the property’s fair market value (less certain liabilities); the shareholder’s basis is that fair market value.
notes.explanation: Liabilities the shareholder assumes, or that the property is subject to, reduce the amount but not below zero.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Amount distributed”, p. 16
notes.evidence: The amount of a distribution is generally the amount of any money paid to the shareholder plus the fair market value (FMV) of any property transferred to the shareholder.

notes.front: A corporation distributes land (adjusted basis $40,000, value $100,000) to a shareholder. Does the corporation recognise gain?
notes.back: Yes: $60,000, generally as if it had sold the land.
notes.explanation: Gain arises when fair market value exceeds adjusted basis: $100,000 − $40,000 = $60,000.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Gain from property distributions”, p. 16
notes.evidence: A corporation will recognize a gain on the distribution of property to a shareholder if the FMV of the property is more than its adjusted basis. This is generally the same treatment the corporation would receive if the property were sold.

notes.front: What DRD percentage generally applies to dividends from a less-than-20%-owned domestic corporation?
notes.explanation: Ownership under 20% puts the dividends on Schedule C, line 1.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule C, Line 1”, p. 18
notes.evidence: Received from less-than-20%-owned domestic corporations subject to income tax, and • Qualified for the 50% deduction under section 243(a)(1).

notes.front: What DRD percentage generally applies to dividends from a domestic corporation the recipient owns 20% or more of?
notes.explanation: The 65% rate is under section 243(c).
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule C, Line 2”, p. 18
notes.evidence: received from 20%-or-more-owned domestic corporations subject to income tax and that are subject to the 65% deduction under section 243(c)

notes.front: Which dividends qualify for the 100% dividends-received deduction?
notes.back: Dividends that qualify under section 243(b), for the deduction described in section 243(a)(3).
notes.explanation: Corporations taking this deduction are subject to section 1561.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule C, Line 16”, p. 21
notes.evidence: Enter only dividends that qualify under section 243(b) for the 100% dividends-received deduction

notes.front: A corporation owns 30% of another domestic corporation and receives $100,000 of dividends from it (no debt-financing). Its taxable income before the DRD is $500,000. What is its DRD?
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: 50% is for less-than-20% ownership. B is wrong: 100% is only for dividends qualifying under section 243(b).
notes.explanation: 30% ownership is 20% or more, so 65% applies: $100,000 × 65% = $65,000. The taxable income limit does not bite: 65% × $500,000 is far above that.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule C, Line 2”, p. 18
notes.evidence: received from 20%-or-more-owned domestic corporations subject to income tax and that are subject to the 65% deduction under section 243(c)

notes.front: What is the general limit on a corporation’s charitable contributions deduction?
notes.back: 10% of taxable income, figured without the contributions deduction and certain other items.
notes.explanation: The items left out include the special deductions on line 29b and NOL and capital loss carrybacks.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Charitable Contributions: Limitation on deduction”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Generally, the total amount claimed cannot be more than 10% of taxable income (line 30) computed without regard to the following. • Any deduction for contributions.

notes.front: What happens to a corporation’s charitable contributions over the 10% limit?
notes.back: They are carried over to the next 5 tax years.
notes.explanation: Exceptions exist for farmers and ranchers and certain Native Corporations.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Charitable Contributions: Carryover”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Charitable contributions over the 10% limitation cannot be deducted for the tax year but can be carried over to the next 5 tax years.

notes.front: A corporation’s 2025 taxable income, before contributions and special deductions, is $200,000; it gave $26,000 to charity. What can it deduct in 2025?
notes.back: C: $20,000, carrying $6,000 forward up to 5 years.
notes.choices:
A) $13,000, carrying $13,000 forward
B) $26,000
C) $20,000, carrying $6,000 forward up to 5 years
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: it ignores the 10% limit. A is wrong: 10% of $200,000 is $20,000, not half the gift.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Charitable Contributions”, p. 14
notes.evidence: Charitable contributions over the 10% limitation cannot be deducted for the tax year but can be carried over to the next 5 tax years.

notes.front: For 2025, how much of taxable income can a corporation’s post-2017 NOL carryovers offset?
notes.back: 80% of taxable income figured without the NOL deduction (and certain other deductions).
notes.explanation: Pre-2018 NOLs carried to the year are not subject to this 80% cap.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Line 29a. Net Operating Loss Deduction”, p. 17
notes.evidence: 80% of the excess, if any, of taxable income determined without any NOL deduction, section 199A deduction, or section 250 deduction, over any NOL carryover to the tax year from tax years beginning before January 1, 2018.

notes.front: A corporation has 2025 taxable income of $100,000 before any NOL deduction and a $150,000 NOL carryover from 2021. How much NOL can it deduct in 2025?
notes.back: B: $80,000, carrying $70,000 forward.
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: a post-2017 NOL can offset only 80% of taxable income.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Line 29a. Net Operating Loss Deduction”, p. 17
notes.evidence: The NOL deduction for tax year 2025 cannot exceed the aggregate amount of NOLs arising in tax years beginning before January 1, 2018, carried to such year plus the lesser of:

notes.front: In which situations is a stock redemption treated as a sale or trade of stock? Name two.
notes.back: Any two, for example: it is not essentially equivalent to a dividend; it is substantially disproportionate.
notes.explanation: Publication 550 also lists a complete redemption of all the shareholder’s stock and certain partial liquidations.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Redemption of stock”, p. 54
notes.evidence: The redemption is treated as a sale or trade of stock if: • The redemption is not essentially equivalent to a dividend

notes.front: A corporation redeems every share an individual owns, for $90,000; her basis is $30,000. How is the redemption treated?
notes.back: C: as a sale, giving $60,000 of capital gain.
notes.choices:
A) As a $90,000 dividend
B) As a tax-free return of capital
C) As a sale, giving $60,000 of capital gain
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a complete redemption of all her stock is treated as a sale. B is wrong: proceeds above basis are gain.
notes.explanation: A complete redemption is on the list of sale treatments: $90,000 − $30,000 = $60,000 gain.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Redemption of stock”, p. 54
notes.evidence: A redemption of stock is treated as a sale or trade and is subject to the capital gain or loss provisions unless the redemption is a dividend or other distribution on stock.

notes.front: When does a liquidating distribution become taxable to a shareholder?
notes.back: Only after they have recovered the basis of their stock; then it is capital gain.
notes.explanation: Whether the gain is long-term or short-term depends on the holding period.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Liquidating Distributions”, p. 31
notes.evidence: Any liquidating distribution you receive is not taxable to you until you have recovered the basis of your stock. After the basis of your stock has been reduced to zero, you must report the liquidating distribution as a capital gain.

notes.front: In a complete liquidation, Sam (stock basis $40,000) receives $25,000 in 2025 and $30,000 in 2026. What does he report each year?
notes.back: C: nothing in 2025; $15,000 capital gain in 2026.
notes.choices:
A) $15,000 loss in 2025; $30,000 gain in 2026
B) $25,000 dividend in 2025; $30,000 dividend in 2026
C) Nothing in 2025; $15,000 capital gain in 2026
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: liquidating distributions are a return of capital, not dividends. A is wrong: no loss arises before the final distribution.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Liquidating Distributions”, p. 31
notes.evidence: Any liquidating distribution you receive is not taxable to you until you have recovered the basis of your stock.

notes.front: If total liquidating distributions are less than stock basis, when can the shareholder report the capital loss?
notes.back: Only after the final liquidating distribution that redeems or cancels the stock.
notes.explanation: Earlier instalments cannot trigger the loss.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Liquidating Distributions”, p. 31
notes.evidence: If the total liquidating distributions you receive are less than the basis of your stock, you may have a capital loss. You can report a capital loss only after you have received the final distribution in liquidation

notes.front: Up to what accumulation is generally treated as within the reasonable needs of most businesses?
notes.explanation: A lower figure applies to certain service businesses.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Accumulated Earnings Tax”, p. 15
notes.evidence: To determine if the corporation is subject to this tax, first treat an accumulation of $250,000 or less generally as

notes.front: What accumulation is treated as within reasonable needs for a business whose main function is services in fields like accounting, law or engineering?
notes.back: $150,000 or less.
notes.explanation: The fields are accounting, actuarial science, architecture, consulting, engineering, health, law and the performing arts.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Accumulated Earnings Tax”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Treat an accumulation of $150,000 or less as within the reasonable needs of a business whose principal function is performing services in the fields of accounting, actuarial science, architecture, consulting, engineering, health (including veterinary services), law, and the performing arts.

notes.front: A law firm corporation has accumulated $200,000 with no specific plans for it. A retail corporation has accumulated $200,000. Which accumulation is within the generally reasonable amount?
notes.back: A: only the retailer’s.
notes.choices:
A) Only the retailer’s
B) Only the law firm’s
C) Both
notes.choicesExplained: C and B are wrong: for a law firm the figure is $150,000, and $200,000 exceeds it.
notes.explanation: The retailer is within $250,000; the law firm’s $200,000 exceeds its $150,000 figure.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Accumulated Earnings Tax”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Treat an accumulation of $150,000 or less as within the reasonable needs of a business whose principal function is performing services in the fields of accounting, actuarial science, architecture, consulting, engineering, health (including veterinary services), law, and the performing arts.

notes.front: Which of these counts as a reasonable need of the business: specific, definite and feasible plans for using the accumulation, or shareholder loans?
notes.back: Specific, definite and feasible plans for using the accumulation in the business.
notes.explanation: Withdrawals by shareholders classed as personal loans may instead indicate there is no bona fide business reason.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Accumulated Earnings Tax”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Specific, definite, and feasible plans for use of the earnings accumulation in the business.

notes.front: When does a corporation generally qualify for the CAMT safe harbor (and so not file Form 4626)?
notes.back: When its average annual adjusted financial statement income for the 3 preceding tax years is under $800 million.
notes.explanation: Special rules apply to members of a controlled group.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Question 29”, p. 28
notes.evidence: Corporations generally qualify for the CAMT safe harbor if the corporation's average annual adjusted financial statement income (AFSI) for the 3 preceding tax years is less than $800 million.

notes.front: Which form figures a corporation’s credit for prior year minimum tax?
notes.back: Form 8827, Credit for Prior Year Minimum Tax—Corporations.
notes.explanation: The allowable credit goes on Schedule J, line 5d, with Form 8827 attached.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1120 (2025), “Schedule J, Line 5d”, p. 22
notes.evidence: Credit for prior year minimum tax. Enter any allowable credit from Form 8827, Credit for Prior Year Minimum Tax—Corporations, line 11. Complete and attach Form 8827.

notes.front: What ownership is “control” for a tax-free exchange of property for stock?
notes.back: At least 80% of total combined voting power and at least 80% of the shares of each class of nonvoting stock, right after the exchange.
notes.explanation: The test can be met by you alone or by your group of transferors.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Control of a corporation”, p. 4
notes.evidence: To be in control of a corporation, you or your group of transferors must own, immediately after the exchange, at least 80% of the total combined voting power of all classes of stock entitled to vote and at least 80% of the outstanding shares of each class of nonvoting stock.

notes.front: Three friends transfer property to an existing corporation and together receive stock giving them 70% of the voting power. Is the exchange tax-free under the control rule?
notes.back: B: no; they need at least 80% after the exchange.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because they act as a group
B) No; they need at least 80% after the exchange
C) Yes, because the corporation already exists
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a group can count together, but 70% is still below 80%. C is wrong: the rule applies to existing corporations too, with the same test.
notes.explanation: Control means at least 80% of voting power (and of each nonvoting class) right after the exchange; 70% falls short.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Control of a corporation”, p. 4
notes.evidence: To be in control of a corporation, you or your group of transferors must own, immediately after the exchange, at least 80% of the total combined voting power

notes.front: In which situations does the tax-free property-for-stock rule not apply? Name two.
notes.back: Any two, for example: the corporation is an investment company; the transfer is in bankruptcy for stock used to pay creditors.
notes.explanation: The third exception is stock received for the corporation’s debt (other than a security), or for interest on its debt that accrued while you held it.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Property Exchanged for Stock”, p. 3
notes.evidence: It does not apply in the following situations. • The corporation is an investment company. • You transfer the property in a bankruptcy or similar proceeding in exchange for stock used to pay creditors.

notes.front: Jo transfers equipment worth $40,000 and does design work worth $5,000 for stock worth $45,000, owning 90% afterwards. What must she report?
notes.back: B: $5,000 of income for the services; no gain on the equipment.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing
B) $5,000 of income for the services; no gain on the equipment
C) $45,000 of income
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: services are not property, so stock for services is income. C is wrong: the equipment exchange qualifies, since she controls the corporation.
notes.explanation: Stock received for services is income to the recipient; the property part stays tax-free.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Services rendered”, p. 28
notes.evidence: The term "property" does not include services rendered or to be rendered to the issuing corporation. The value of stock received for services is income to the recipient.

notes.front: Are services rendered to a corporation “property” for the tax-free exchange rules?
notes.back: No. The value of stock received for services is income to the recipient.
notes.explanation: This covers services already rendered or to be rendered.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Services rendered”, p. 28
notes.evidence: The term "property" does not include services rendered or to be rendered to the issuing corporation.

notes.front: In a section 351 exchange where boot is received, what is the most gain recognised?
notes.back: The amount of money plus the fair market value of the other property received.
notes.explanation: A loss cannot be recognised or deducted.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Money or other property received”, p. 28
notes.evidence: You must recognize gain only up to the amount of money plus the FMV of the other property you receive.

notes.front: Ray transfers land (basis $20,000, value $50,000) for 100% of a new corporation’s stock worth $40,000 plus $10,000 cash. What gain does he recognise?
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: that is the realised gain, but recognition is capped by the boot. A is wrong: the cash boot triggers gain.
notes.explanation: Realised gain is $50,000 − $20,000 = $30,000; recognised gain is capped at the $10,000 of money received.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Money or other property received”, p. 28
notes.evidence: You must recognize gain only up to the amount of money plus the FMV of the other property you receive.

notes.front: In a section 351 exchange, the corporation assumes a $70,000 mortgage on a building whose adjusted basis is $50,000 (good business reason, no avoidance purpose). Result?
notes.back: $20,000 of gain: liabilities assumed exceed adjusted basis by that much.
notes.explanation: Otherwise, assuming liabilities is generally not treated as receiving money.
notes.source: Publication 544 (2025), Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets, “Liabilities”, p. 28
notes.evidence: If the liabilities the corporation assumes are more than your adjusted basis in the property you transfer, gain is recognized up to the difference.

notes.front: In a tax-free exchange of property for stock, what is the shareholder’s basis in the stock received?
notes.back: Generally the adjusted basis of the property transferred, adjusted for cash, other property, gain or loss and liabilities assumed.
notes.explanation: Gain recognised increases it; cash and the value of other property received decrease it.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Basis of stock or other property received”, p. 4
notes.evidence: The basis of the stock you receive is generally the adjusted basis of the property you transfer. Increase this amount by any amount treated as a dividend, plus any gain recognized on the exchange.

notes.front: What is the corporation’s basis in property it receives for its stock?
notes.back: Generally the transferor’s basis, increased by any gain the transferor recognised.
notes.explanation: The increase for recognised gain may be limited under section 362.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Basis of property transferred”, p. 4
notes.evidence: A corporation that receives property from you in exchange for its stock generally has the same basis you had in the property, increased by any gain you recognized on the exchange.

notes.front: Are contributions to a corporation’s capital generally taxable to the corporation?
notes.back: No. They are paid-in capital and not taxable to the corporation.
notes.explanation: But nonshareholder contributions made after 22 December 2017 by a civic group, a governmental entity or a customer (in aid of construction) are not nontaxable paid-in capital.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Capital Contributions”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Generally, contributions to the capital of a corporation, whether or not by shareholders, are paid-in capital. These contributions are not taxable to the corporation.

notes.front: In a parent–subsidiary controlled group, what share of each subsidiary must be owned within the group?
notes.back: At least 80% of total voting power or at least 80% of total value of its stock.
notes.explanation: The corporations are chained through stock ownership to a common parent.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule O (Form 1120) (Rev. December 2018), “Parent–subsidiary group”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Stock possessing at least 80% of the total combined voting power of all classes of stock entitled to vote or at least 80% of the total value of shares of all classes of stock of each of the corporations, except the common parent corporation

notes.front: In a brother–sister controlled group, who must own the corporations, and what ownership tests apply?
notes.back: The same five or fewer individuals, estates or trusts, meeting an 80% test and a more-than-50% test.
notes.explanation: The 50% test counts each person’s ownership only where it is identical across the corporations.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule O (Form 1120) (Rev. December 2018), “Brother–sister group”, p. 2
notes.evidence: two or more corporations where the same five or fewer persons who are individuals, estates, or trusts directly or indirectly own stock possessing:

notes.front: Alpha Inc. owns 85% of the voting stock of Beta Inc. What must Beta (and Alpha) file with their returns?
notes.back: A: Schedule O, as component members of a controlled group.
notes.choices:
A) Schedule O, as component members of a controlled group
B) Form 8832, to elect a classification
C) Nothing extra: each corporation is separate
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: Form 8832 is for eligible entities choosing a classification. C is wrong: an 80%-or-more parent–subsidiary link makes them a controlled group.
notes.explanation: 85% of voting power meets the 80% test, so the two form a parent–subsidiary group.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule O (Form 1120) (Rev. December 2018), “Parent–subsidiary group”, p. 1
notes.evidence: A corporation that is a component member (defined below) of a controlled group must use Schedule O to report the apportionment of certain tax benefits between all component members of the group.

notes.front: Four individuals own 60% of a retail corporation’s stock by value all year; 200 others own the rest. Is it closely held?
notes.back: Yes. Five or fewer individuals own over 50% by value in the year’s last half, and it is not a personal service corporation.
notes.explanation: Both conditions in Publication 542 are met.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Closely held corporations”, p. 3
notes.evidence: It is not a personal service corporation. 2. At any time during the last half of the tax year, more than 50% of the value of its outstanding stock is, directly or indirectly, owned by or for five or fewer individuals.

notes.front: For a personal service corporation, what two tests about employee-owners must be met?
notes.back: Over 20% of personal-service compensation cost is for their services, and they own over 10% of the stock’s value.
notes.explanation: The stock test is measured on the last day of the testing period.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Personal service corporations”, p. 3
notes.evidence: This requirement is met if more than 20% of the corporation's compensation cost for its activities of performing personal services during the testing period is for personal services performed by employee-owners. 3. Its employee-owners own more than 10% of the fair market value of its outstanding stock

notes.front: Which activity is not a “personal service” for the personal service corporation rules?
notes.back: A: retail sales.
notes.choices:
A) Retail sales
B) Veterinary services
C) Architecture
notes.choicesExplained: C and B are wrong: architecture and health (including veterinary services) are both listed fields.
notes.explanation: Personal services cover accounting, actuarial science, architecture, consulting, engineering, health, law and the performing arts.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Personal services”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Personal services include any activity performed in the fields of accounting, actuarial science, architecture, consulting, engineering, health (including veterinary services), law, and the performing arts.

notes.front: A consulting firm owned and staffed by its three consultants meets the personal service corporation tests. Can it also be a closely held corporation?
notes.back: No. A closely held corporation must not be a personal service corporation.
notes.explanation: Being a personal service corporation is checked first; only other corporations can be closely held.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Closely held corporations”, p. 3
notes.evidence: A corporation is closely held if all of the following apply. 1. It is not a personal service corporation.

notes.front: Lara owns 60% of a corporation’s stock by value and sells it land at a $12,000 loss. Can she deduct the loss?
notes.back: No. She is a related person (over 50%), and losses between related persons are denied.
notes.explanation: An individual owning more than 50% of the stock’s value, directly or indirectly, is related to the corporation.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Related Persons”, p. 9
notes.evidence: These rules also deny the deduction of losses on the sale or exchange of property between related persons. Related persons. For purposes of this rule, the following persons are related to a corporation.

notes.front: Two corporations each distribute $10,000; one has ample E&P and the other none. How does the shareholders’ treatment differ?
notes.back: From E&P it is a dividend; without E&P it reduces stock basis, with any excess taxed as gain.
notes.explanation: E&P decides the character of a distribution, not its amount.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Reporting Dividends and Other Distributions”, p. 17
notes.evidence: Any part of a distribution from either current or accumulated earnings and profits is reported to the shareholder as a dividend. Any part of a distribution that is not from earnings and profits is applied against and reduces the adjusted basis of the stock
